book.t: "Under the sun": a phrase used about thirty times in Ecclesiastes for life in this world as seen from a purely earthly point of view.

1:1.t: "The Teacher": the KJV's "the Preacher", Hebrew Qoheleth, one who gathers an assembly and speaks to it. The Greek title Ecclesiastes comes from the same idea.

1:14.t: "A chase after the wind": the KJV's "vexation of spirit". The Hebrew re'ut ruach means striving after wind, as useless as trying to catch the wind. Ruach means both "wind" and "spirit".

2:8.t: "Musical instruments of every kind": following the KJV. The Hebrew shiddah veshiddot occurs only here, and its meaning is uncertain; many modern readers take it as "many concubines".

2:25.t: "More than I": following the KJV and the standard Hebrew. Some Hebrew manuscripts and the Greek and Syriac read "apart from Him", that is, without God no one can eat or find enjoyment.

3:21.t: The KJV reads "the spirit of man that goeth upward, and the spirit of the beast that goeth downward". The Hebrew can be read as a question, "Who knows whether...?", as here. The Teacher's answer comes in 12:7: the spirit returns to God who gave it.

4:5.t: "Ruins himself": the KJV's "eateth his own flesh".

4:13.t: The Hebrew of this passage is difficult, and the identity of the youth and the "second" is unclear.

5:1.t: "Guard your steps": the KJV's "Keep thy foot". In the Hebrew this is 4:17, and 5:1-20 is 5:2-21.

5:6.t: "The messenger": the KJV's "the angel"; Hebrew malakh, probably the priest who received vows (Malachi 2:7).

6:3.t: "A stillborn child": the KJV's "an untimely birth".

7:1.t: "A good name is better than fine perfume": a wordplay in Hebrew, shem (name) and shemen (perfume).

7:6.t: "The crackling of thorns": thorns flare up quickly with a loud noise but give little heat.

7:18.t: "Will avoid all extremes": the KJV's "shall come forth of them all".

7:26.t: The Teacher describes what he found in his own search among the people he knew; it is an observation of human corruption, summed up in verse 29, not a teaching that women are worse than men (see Proverbs 31:10).

8:10.t: The Hebrew of this verse is uncertain.

10:2.t: "Right ... left": in the ancient world the right side stood for skill and favor, the left for clumsiness and misfortune.

10:16.t: "Was a servant": the KJV's "is a child". The Hebrew na'ar can mean either.

11:1.t: "Send your bread out upon the waters": probably a picture of seagoing trade, or of generous giving that returns in time.

12:3.t: A picture of old age: "the keepers of the house" are the hands, "the strong men" the legs, "the grinders" the teeth, "those looking through the windows" the eyes, and the white-flowering almond tree the gray hair.

12:6.t: "The silver cord ... the golden bowl": a lamp hanging from a cord; when the cord breaks the bowl falls and the light goes out, a picture of death.

1:2.t: "Fleeting" (Hebrew hevel): the KJV's "vanity". Hevel means a breath or vapor, something brief and impossible to grasp. It is used thirty-eight times in the book. "Utterly fleeting" renders the Hebrew superlative havel havalim, "breath of breaths", the KJV's "vanity of vanities". The word does not mean that life is worthless, but that it is passing and beyond human control. Abel's name is the same word (Genesis 4:2).

3:11.t: "Eternity" (Hebrew ha'olam): the KJV's "the world". God has placed in people a sense of what lasts beyond time, a longing no earthly thing can satisfy.

4:12.t: "A cord of three strands": a picture of the strength of companionship. Many Christian weddings apply it to a husband and wife bound together with God.

5:2.t: "God is in heaven and you are on earth": a call to reverent, few words in prayer. Jesus taught the same (Matthew 6:7).

5:15.t: "Naked from their mother's womb": see Job 1:21 and 1 Timothy 6:7.

7:20.t: "No one on earth who is righteous ... and never sins": Paul makes the same point in Romans 3:10-12.

7:29.t: "Schemes" (Hebrew chishshevonot): the KJV's "inventions". God made people upright, but they have devised many ways of their own. See Genesis 1:31 and 3.

8:8.t: "Over the wind" (Hebrew ruach): the KJV reads "power over the spirit to retain the spirit". Ruach means both wind and the breath of life.

9:5.t: "The dead know nothing": spoken from the viewpoint "under the sun", of what the dead can do or know in this world. It is not a full teaching on the afterlife; see 12:7 and 12:14.

12:1.t: "Your Creator" (Hebrew bor'ekha): from bara, the verb of Genesis 1:1. Remember the One who made you while you are young and strong.

12:7.t: "The spirit returns to God who gave it" (Hebrew ruach): the breath of life God breathed into man (Genesis 2:7) goes back to Him. Compare 3:21.

12:11.t: "One Shepherd": God, the source of true wisdom. Goads prod oxen forward; nails hold firm. Wise words both spur and steady.

12:13.t: "The whole duty of every person": literally "this is the whole of man". After all the searching "under the sun", the conclusion is reverence for God and obedience to Him.
